headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers, one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, not a general comparison of the two conditions.

The Lyme disease paper reports diagnostic-delay and hospitalization figures but no cost, insurance, or income-loss data, while the Long COVID paper reports national and demographic prevalence figures but no cost, delay, or severity data either.
Neither source document contains any direct medical cost, productivity-loss, or caregiving-time figures, so no financial-burden comparison between the two conditions is possible from this evidence.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports a mean time from symptom onset to diagnosis of 16.5 days overall, 24.9 days for disseminated-disease cases, and 13.4 days for EM-only cases.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper contains no diagnostic-delay measure; it reports only self-reported ever/current prevalence.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Diagnostic-timing evidence exists only for Lyme disease in this comparison, so no side-by-side delay comparison is possible.

comparison_rows.dimension: Out-of-pocket and direct medical cost evidence

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper states that out-of-pocket costs, insurance coverage, travel or non-medical costs, and caregiving time are not mentioned anywhere in the document.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper likewise reports no direct medical or non-medical cost figures of any kind; it is strictly a prevalence survey.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Cost evidence is absent from both source documents, so neither paper can support a dollar-based burden estimate on its own.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper does not mention lost income, missed work, or productivity loss, even though it describes symptoms like malaise and difficulty concentrating in qualitative terms.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper contains no data on lost income, missed work, or productivity; it measures only whether someone ever or currently has Long COVID.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Work and income loss is unmeasured in both source documents, so financial burden from paid-work disruption cannot be compared across the two conditions here.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper states there is no data on insurance status or access barriers across the six countries studied.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper contains no data on healthcare utilization, treatment-seeking patterns, or insurance/access barriers for the people captured in its prevalence estimates.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Access-barrier evidence is missing from both source documents, limiting what either paper can say about affordability of care.

comparison_rows.dimension: Demographic or subgroup breakdown of burden

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper's diagnostic-delay figure (16.5 days) is broken down only by clinical manifestation type, not by sex, age, or any demographic subgroup, and the document does not state that subgroup variation was checked and found negligible.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper breaks prevalence down by sex, age group, race/Hispanic origin, family income, and urbanization level, reporting specific gaps such as a 3.3 percentage-point higher ever-prevalence in women than men and a 4.8 percentage-point higher ever-prevalence in ages 35-49 than ages 65 and older.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two source documents disaggregate burden along very different dimensions (clinical manifestation versus demographic subgroup), so their subgroup findings are not directly comparable.

comparison_rows.dimension: How each condition's official data is limited

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper notes that European surveillance of Lyme borreliosis manifestations has been limited by differing diagnostic practices across countries, with EU-level standardized surveillance for neuroborreliosis only beginning in 2018, which is why the underlying study built its own harmonized case definitions.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not describe a systemic surveillance limitation of this kind; it reports a single self-reported 2022 national prevalence measure without flagging an equivalent dated surveillance gap.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper names a specific, dated systemic limitation in official surveillance in this comparison.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports a hospitalization rate of 1.3 percent among enrolled cases and a disseminated-disease proportion of 22.8 percent among all medically attended cases.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper contains no severity or hospitalization measure, only ever/current prevalence percentages.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Severity evidence of this kind is only available for Lyme disease in this comparison.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports cohort case counts (315 enrolled, 797 medically attended cases) from 14 practices in Lyme-endemic regions of six countries, not a national or general-population prevalence rate.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports that 6.9 percent of U.S. adults ever had Long COVID and 3.4 percent currently had it in 2022, based on a national survey.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two source documents measure scale in fundamentally different ways (endemic-region clinical cohort versus national self-reported prevalence), so their population figures should not be treated as equivalent.

shared_themes.theme: Neither source document behind these two papers provides any cost, insurance-access, or productivity-loss figures, leaving a complete financial-burden gap for both conditions in this comparison.

evidence.note: States explicitly that out-of-pocket costs, insurance coverage, travel/non-medical costs, caregiving time, and lost income/productivity are not mentioned anywhere in the document.
States it is strictly a self-reported prevalence survey with no dollar costs, direct or indirect financial burden, insurance/access barriers, or caregiving burden reported.

shared_themes.theme: Both source documents point to further burden-relevant evidence that lies outside what is reported here, rather than quantifying it themselves.

evidence.note: Notes that post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome and patient-reported outcome findings from the same cohort will be published in separate manuscripts not included in this document.
Cites an external reference for long-term health and economic impacts of Long COVID without quantifying any such impact itself.

condition_specific_themes.theme: Diagnostic delay for Lyme disease differs sharply by how the disease presents, with disseminated cases diagnosed markedly later than EM-only cases.

evidence.note: Reports a mean diagnostic delay of 24.9 days for disseminated disease versus 13.4 days for EM-only cases, an 11.5-day gap.

condition_specific_themes.theme: Antibiotic treatment duration for Lyme disease varies widely by country rather than following one standard course.

evidence.note: Reports a median treatment duration of 23.5 days in Poland versus 9 days in Slovakia, a 14.5-day country-level gap.

condition_specific_themes.theme: Long COVID prevalence in this paper's source data varies by demographic subgroup rather than being evenly distributed across the population.

evidence.note: Reports ever-prevalence ranging from 8.9 percent in ages 35-49 to 4.1 percent in ages 65 and older, and from 8.3 percent in Hispanic adults to 2.6 percent in Asian non-Hispanic adults.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither source document behind these two papers includes any direct medical cost, indirect cost, or caregiving-time data, so no cost-of-illness comparison can be built from this evidence alone.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers two papers, one built from a European Lyme disease surveillance study and one built from a U.S. national Long COVID prevalence survey, and it does not describe either condition in general. The Lyme disease paper offers diagnostic-delay, hospitalization, and treatment-duration figures but no cost, insurance, or income-loss data, while the Long COVID paper offers national and demographic prevalence figures but no delay, severity, or cost data. The one shared pattern that can be shown with real figures is that both source documents are silent on direct and indirect costs, access barriers, and productivity loss. Because there is exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, and no paper covering both conditions, every row above reflects what these two specific documents happen to report rather than a broader claim about either condition.
cross_analysis.limitations: This is a small, non-random sample built from whichever documents happened to be uploaded: 1 Lyme disease paper and 1 Long COVID paper, with no paper covering both conditions, as given in the real figures. It is not a controlled study, and agreement or disagreement between these two papers does not validate either one; findings reflect only what each specific source document reports.

learning_cards.headline: Severity may delay diagnosis; worth checking for Long COVID too
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper reports a diagnostic delay gap of 11.5 days, with disseminated disease diagnosed later than EM-only disease.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper, as summarized here, does not measure diagnostic delay or any time-to-diagnosis figure at all.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers check whether people with more severe or multi-system presentations are diagnosed later than those with milder, single-symptom presentations?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper shows that how a condition presents can be linked to how long diagnosis takes, a question the Long COVID paper's current figures cannot yet address; neither paper offers cost or access data the other could borrow from in return.
